maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to move an amendment to this motion, but before reading my amendment I have a few remarks to make. The amendment deals with the question of levies or alleged levies made in connection with Canadian National Railways contracts. I hasten to add that I am fully aware of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) appears to believe that I am rather insistent upon this point, but he may hold that opinion simply because I have never yet had the opportunity of expressing exactly what I have in mind, and that I propose to do now.
I am introducing an amendment at this time because there should be absolutely no delay with reference to so grave a matter. Just picture the situation: an hon. member declares to the house that he knows that certain levies are being made in connection with contracts of the Canadian National Railways. Before making that definite statement he had said that political corruption was never so rampant in Canada, and it was while emphasizing that particular point that he mentioned the Canadian National Railways. To anyone who desires to know the truth, what do these statements mean?
I believe we should refer again to what has been said in this house in order to get a clear picture of the situation. For example, we find this statement:
Never in the history of this country has corruption been so rampant electorally as it is to-day. It is not a case of $5,000 or $10,000 in a constituency, but it is a case of large sums of money for corrupt purposes.
We go on a bit further and we find this:
When an organizer goes to a contractor and says that he wants one or ten per cent, that is a levy and not a contribution. What is more, I say that it threatens the very life of this state at this moment.	.
And further on we find this:
In view of what I know of the character of the methods by which contributions are made -they are no longer contributions but levies-
I pause here to underline the words "no longer." When a member makes a statement
Corrupt Electoral Practices

to the effect that these are no longer contributions it conveys the idea that some time in the past things were different. He is saying that to his knowledge at the present time things are no longer what they used to be-they are no longer contributions, but levies. Further, he says:
I say the time has come when we must provide methods under our electoral law which will not permit such a situation to continue.
Further on we find these words:
A contribution is one thing, but a levy of
a certain per cent is another. The time has come when this must stop because the contractors themselves are complaining.
If this does not imply that the right hon. member who made the statement knows definitely whereof he speaks, then my knowledge of the English language is not as perfect as I think it is. But in order to prove definitely that he really meant a good deal, we find the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) saying to the right hon. leader of the opposition :
The right hon. gentleman has said either too much or too little.
And at that very moment, as all members of the house will recall, there arose an anxious cry throughout the house for the government to set up a committee, and my hon. friend from Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), whom I do not see in his seat at the moment, was the very first one to say: Let us have one "right now." Therefore at that particular time it was definitely understood that there certainly was something very wrong. Let us see what the Minister of Transport said:
Mr. Howe: As one who places a great many contracts for this government I ask the right hon. gentleman to give me a specific instance of a levy.
Mr. Bennett:	I can give the minister as
many as he wants, but I am not going to do it here and now.
Then here is the important part. The leader of the opposition went on to say:
What is more, I know of levies being made in connection with Canadian National Railways contracts.
Further on we have the right hon. leader of the opposition saying this:
It can be threshed out any time you want any committee of this house that you desire to appoint to go into the matter.
It was then that the hon. member for Cochrane interjected, "right now."
It may be all right, Mr. Speaker, to try to hide behind words, but when I heard those statements of the right hon. leader of the opposition-and I have gone over them very carefully-I had the definite impression that

a certain meaning was to be attached to them, and I know definitely what meaning the people of this country are attaching to them. When the right hon. leader of the opposition makes a statement to the effect that ward bosses and political organizers have developed such a boldness'of approach that their demands are no longer simply demands but amount to levies upon contractors, then I think it is time this house looked into the matter.
But the right hon. leader of the opposition did not stop there. He even named the amount of the levies in a case he knew about, and he said they had reached such proportions that even the contractors themselves were complaining. Now, those words of his are perfectly clear. They mean exactly what they would have meant if said outside this house or if printed elsewhere than upon the pages of Hansard.
When I heard those statements, Mr. Speaker,
I did the only thing I thought I should do. I got up in the house and asked the Prime Minister if it was his intention to set up a committee to investigate the charges, and in a prepared statement the Prime Minister replied in this vein. He first reviewed the various statutes of Canada under which charges of alleged political corruption may be investigated. He pointed out that parliament had made statutory provision for the investigation of corrupt practices at elections. There was the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, chapter 50, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, under which, he said,
-any person who has the right to vote may present a petition to a judge of a supreme or superior court, setting out these practices, and, if a deposit of $1,000 is made, an investigation may be held.
That is one method which the Prime Minister said could be followed to investigate the charges of the ri^ht hon. leader of the opposition. There was also a second way, Which the Prime Minister outlined as follows:
Under the Corrupt Practices Act, chapter 51, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, twenty-five or more electors may present a petition to the House of Commons charging the existence of such practices, and, if a deposit of $1,000 is made-
Again I point to the SI,000-
-the house may direct the government to appoint a commission for the purpose of making an inquiry. The commisison in either case must submit a report to parliament and under standing order No. 79 it is provided that if it appears that any person lias been elected by corrupt practices the house will proceed with the utmost severity.
Before pointing out these steps that might be taken the Prime Minister was very careful to remark that as I was a young member of

Corrupt Electoral Practices
the house possibly I was not familiar with the procedure in connection with charges of this kind. In reply I simply state, Mr. Speaker, that it is possible to know everything and yet understand nothing. I am not concerned with questions of law, nor do I propose to permit legalities to stand in my way. I cannot consider that such legal steps must be necessary or even advisable when all that needs to be done is for the house to appoint a committee of inquiry into the charges of the right hon. leader of the opposition.
Furthermore, we already have our standing committee on privileges and elections, and we all know that any question, whether concrete or academic, may be referred to a committee of this house fully empowered to investigate it.
It might also be suggested that the public accounts committee could very well look after this matter. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that we are not now dealing with one particular charge, as was mentioned by the Prime Minister; we are dealing with something which is undermining the political life of our dominion, and the scope of the public accounts committee is too narrow, in my opinion, to enable them to investigate a matter of this kind as it should be investigated.
I would also ask this question: Why should the responsibility be placed upon the public? In order to clear away this stigma on the house it seems to me that the Prime Minister and the government should move heaven and earth to find a method by which these charges can be cleared up. I know the Prime Minister to be a man of honesty and courage. I know him to be a man who does not hesitate to perform the task before him, but sometimes I think he might flinch and be reluctant to take action in a matter of this kind because he sees upon the horizon, perhaps, the shadow of another Beauharnois. I do not know, but if such should be the case, knowing the Prime Minister as well as I do, I am sure he realizes as everybody does that these charges have gone out to the country and to the people who have sent us here, and I think that the Prime Minister will help me out and do all he can to see that the people of Canada are well informed in the matter.
If the Prime Minister sees these threatening shadows upon the horizon, may I say to him that I sympathize with him and will do all I can to help him ward off any blows that may come; but if blows should come, let us face them fearlessly, let them fall where they may. I sympathize with the Prime Minister because he is not only the leader of the Liberal party but also the prime minister of all the people of Canada, and should corrupt practices be found to exist elsewhere than in
the Liberal party I know that will grieve him just as much as if they were found within the ranks of his own party. If we allow these clouds to remain over this house, great will be the people's wonderment; they may begin to ask themselves whether we in this parliament have lost in a cloud of personal fear, the traditions of those who came before us. and they may lose their last glimmer of faith in our political life.
What of the youth of this country? The allegations made by the leader of the opposition have been read right across Canada and have definitely left an impression on the minds of the young people. Are we going to smash the idealism which they possess at the present time, destroy their faith in our institutions and our political life by hushing up these charges and letting them go untried? We should not be doing our duty towards the youth of this country if we permitted such a thing to continue.
I do not intend to discuss this question at great length-

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
-because I feel that it is unnecessary. Some hon. members say "hear, hear." Perhaps that is the way they feel about it, but I believe they thereby indicate that they do not fully recognize their duty to those who sent them to this house. They should be more ready to support me in a matter of this kind.
I have a plea to make to-day. I make it on behalf of the people in general but especially on behalf of the youth of this country, and even in the interest of those who have to pay the deficits on the Canadian National Railways. I ask the members of the House of Commons to see to it that the stigma which clouds this house at the present time is swept away. Before we begin to look after somebody else's business affairs we should see to it that our own skirts are kept clean, and make it clear that we know what we are talking about. Therefore I take pleasure in moving the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by leaving out all the words in the motion after "that" and the following be inserted:
This house is of the opinion that charges of levies in connection with Canadian National Railways contracts as well as statements concerning electoral corruption should be referred to a select committee of this house with power to send for papers, persons and witnesses and to take evidence under oath and to report to this house.
Corrupt Electoral Practices

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
On February 1, I spoke against corruption. I pointed out that money and propaganda were used to deceive the people; that consequently the will of those who were struggling to have their desires expressed in and carried out by their governments was being overridden by secret, hidden influences that were apparently drawing their support from the wages of corruption; that red herrings were being dragged across the trail in a great many constituencies throughout this country, with the deliberate object of confusing the people. Among other things, I condemned the People's League for its activity in Alberta last summer. I pointed out with reference to the Lethbridge by-election that, strange as it may seem, the People's League was able to hold together until the election was achieved and that then the leader of the Liberal party immediately withdrew; and everybody who has been thinking at all about that matter has wondered why in the name of common sense the Liberal leader did not give the people of Lethbridge a ghost of a chance and make his statement three days before the election instead of three days after. This thing has offended and disgusted to a greater degree more people than hon. members have any conception of, because the object of the whole intrigue-shall we call it

was so manifest.
I believe that hon. members would be interested in a further development of the Lethbridge by-election. I am going to read to them, in case they have not seen it, a passage from the Lethbridge Herald of February 5, 1938, page 4. It is an editorial, and I am quoting it because it indicates the kind of thing with which we in Alberta are confronted all the time.
Perhaps the advertisements appearing in the Herald on Wednesday setting forth the campaign expenses of Doctor Campbell and A. J. Burnap in the recent by-election tell the true story. Perhaps they are a little misleading. The figures show that Doctor Campbell's committee spent $1,049, while Mr. Burnap's committee spent $237.
The figures of course do not take into account a few rather important facts.
Before I read further may I ask hon. members to weigh quickly in their minds, as I know they can do, the principles which the Lethbridge Herald is laying down in the following words:
They do not show how much it cost the taxpayers of Alberta for Premier Aberhart to make two trips to Lethbridge and spend practically a week here during the campaign.

Are we to assume that the premier of a province is not supposed to go out and do what he can towards enlightening the people as to his point of view?
No doubt Mr. Aberhart was drawing his salary of some $200 a week during that time. No doubt also Hon. Mr. Low, Hon. Mr. Tanner, Hon. Doctor Cross, Hon. Mr. Maynard and Hon. Mr. Manning, who receive from the taxpayers of Alberta some $150 a week, also drew their salaries while they were campaigning here.
I wonder if there is not an intimation there that these gentlemen were not going to do a full year's work because, upon the invitation of the people of Lethbridge, they spent a few days in the constituency.
Mr. Speaker Dawson and Mr. Popil, two members of the legislature, also helped in the campaign. No doubt the expense accounts of the various members of Mr. Aberhart's ministry would show that they had very important business in Lethbridge during the election campaign.
The insinuation is obvious.
We leave it to the people of Alberta to judge whether the social credit campaign in the by-election cost only $237.
In view of such remarks as were made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and in view of such evidence as comes pouring in from a wide variety of directions, to strain at a gnat and swallow a camel, as is indicated by this editorial, must strike any calm mind as being utterly revolting and disgusting.
So much by way of beginning. I should like once more to make it perfectly clear, as I endeavoured to do in my speech on February 1, that I am in favour of election reform. At that time I pointed out the way in which, since 1921, Alberta has grappled with this problem, teaching its citizens to form great people's organizations and contribute the money with which they fought their campaigns; to keep an open account in order to show where the money came from, how much they had, how it was spent and all those matters which are so necessary to keep an electorate informed and satisfied that those who are chosen to represent them are not in the pay of certain big interests. As I also pointed out, it repels us to think that, after all the effort we have put forth, which cost the people of our province an incalculable amount in anxiety, in money that they could ill spare, and in various other ways, the results should be overborne or nullified by people who are assisted from nobody knows where.
I contend that what the leader of the opposition implied is, as regards this country, absolutely true. If democracy is to continue in

Corrupt Electoral Practices
Canada, we must have wholesale, genuine and thoroughgoing repentance on the part of all the leading organizations who stand for election to the governing bodies of this country as well as on the part of all who stand behind the organizations. In what I have to say there is nothing personal and nothing partisan. Both parties must change. I am not deceived into thinking that because the leader of the opposition made the charge, or the intimated charge, the other side is therefore the only one that is blameworthy. I think it is a fairly good illustration of the old saying about the pot calling the kettle black. I believe that the history of both sides going back a few generations in Canada will reveal a sufficient number of unsightly incidents to make each party very reticent about levelling charges against the other. And I say this realizing fully that the present leader of the opposition and the present leader of the government may be completely innocent; indeed, I am inclined to believe that they both are. It is not their desire in any way to condone this sort of thing. What we must do, however, is to make matters different so that they will have a chance to lead the country without such intimations being thrown out and such unsightly things occurring.
It seems to me that there is a giant octopus hidden somewhere, and it is nourished somewhere near the centre of Canada. It extends long, hidden, treacherous tentacles wherever the people begin to get any sort of insight into the truth and any sort of idea of what to do about it. Whenever that happens it quietly and clandestinely strangles any movement which the people have built up. What is the cause of this? There is little use in our railing against the malady unless we seek the cause. Railing against the malady until you learn the cause and endeavour to remove it is as profitable as trying to cure smallpox by painting over or scratching off the pimples. Let us see if we can find out what the cause of the difficulty is.
Personally I believe that the first cause of the trouble is bewilderment. There exists uncertainty among the people of Canada. As a new member of parliament, I judge that it is because of the great amount of misinformation that exists everywhere throughout the country, and the misunderstanding, delusion and prejudice. If any hon. member of this house thinks he can successfully challenge the statement that throughout Canada there exists a great amount of misinformation, misunderstanding, delusion and prejudice, then it will be interesting to hear his defence. On top of all this and aggravating the whole situation there is selfishness everywhere at work
confounding the confusion. Each party is in a false position. I believe it was the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham) who last year read a letter that was rather interesting. I am not saying that I entirely agree with what was in that letter, but there was in it a thought-provoking passage. The writer said that the Liberals have been false to true principles while the Conservatives have been true to false principles. The result is that, of course, the country has suffered all these generations.
Inasmuch as I am of Liberal tendencies myself, and inasmuch as I find that in consequence the Liberal members of the house have been and are now, shall I say, more congenial- or perhaps I understand them better-may I talk to the Liberal members for a few minutes. In the first place, are the Liberals to-day false to true principles?

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Let us not answer the question too readily. It is easy to answer it at once; but, are they? Let us discuss the question for a moment or two. Someone asks, who is to judge? Well, before you decide who is to judge, the first thing to do is to fix upon a standard of judgment, and that is what we shall have to do now. In the first place, Liberals for some generations have, at least ostensibly, committed themselves to the principles of laissez-faire.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: By no means.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
If they have not committed themselves to the principles of laissez-faire let us acknowledge it frankly before the people so that everyone will know exactly where the Liberal party does stand. One of the chief reasons for the difficulty that faces us to-day is that no one knows where either party stands, and apparently each party is studiously and assiduously endeavouring to prevent everybody from finding out.
Let us deal with the question of laissez-faire. Laissez-faire involves four fundamental principles: first, free trade; second, free export of capital; third, no interference with contracts between employer and employee, or free association; and fourth, a metallic currency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Whose definition is that?

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
What Canada is
waiting to hear is a definition from someone in the Liberal party-a definition other than this. It only illustrates what I said a moment ago. We want to find out where these parties do stand; we want to know what the difference is between the Liberal party of to-day
Corrupt Electoral Practices

and the Liberal party of fifty years ago. When we know that we shall be in a position to judge.
Let us consider to what extent the Liberal party to-day agrees with these four principles and to what extent the principles themselves can be accepted. The first is free trade.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
What about social
credit?

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Some hon. members
are anxious to hear about social credit. When we turn on the social credit guns they will wish they were not hearing about it. A most interesting statement-interesting not only to all parties in this house but to the people throughout the country-is to be found in the words of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) when, speaking on February 7, he said:
You cannot move to extremes in tariff policy without endangering national unity and without undermining the very foundations of federal public finance.
In other words, the principle of free trade apparently has gone by the board. The next question is, what is going to be the effect on the people when a man who has been an avowed free trader stands up in his place in parliament and makes such a statement? The effect is to destroy the confidence of the people in that man and in the party. There is no escaping that conclusion and the result is great chaos in ideas. For instance, suppose we take the question of sugar. I will discuss that question to illustrate the present chaotic thinking among the parties. Does the Liberal party as a party favour the protection of the sugar industry, or does it not? If it favours the protection of the sugar industry then it favours the protection of other industries; if it does not favour the protection of the sugar industry how can it favour the protection of others? The result is that, since we are not able to give consistent answers to these questions, we are simply in a state of chaos so far as the whole question of protection and free trade is concerned.

speechtext:
All	these things
indicate why there is graft in Canada. I say that the chief reason for graft is simply the fact that neither party dares to come out before the Canadian people and tell them what it stands for. The result is that they try by every means to get power, regardless

of what they will do when they get in, or what the people think they are going to do, or what the people demand, or what the effect is going to be on the morale of the people. All they are concerned about is getting into power. The chief cause of this result is this very thing I am talking about; consequently I maintain that this is strictly bearing out what I set out to say.
As a liberal party what are we going to say regarding price spreads? Western Canada suffers the gravest disadvantage and disability in that connection, because the people out there sell their produce in an unprotected market, while everything they require in order to produce those goods they have to buy in a protected market. For instance, the manufacturers of agricultural implements during the depression cut their prices only six per cent and limited their production so that they would be able to sell all they produced at a tremendously high price, while the farmer who must have agricultural implements in order to be able to produce his wheat saw his prices forced down and down and down according to world market conditions until he was producing a great deal more wheat than before the depression-or trying to-and therefore forcing the price level further down. Until that situation is faced frankly and dealt with by parliament in an effective way, there can never be justice between east and west. That is just one example. Where does the Liberal party stand on that, and what is it going to do? Nobody knows. The result is a great deal of attempted deception, and this very kind of corruption or attempted corruption which we are discussing to-day.
The next principle of laissez-faire is the export of capital. I am not going into that in any great detail, but I want to show how greatly the people become confused by all this. Capital, we are told, is exported to enable us to export goods, and the idea is that if we have free trade and get plenty of export markets war will be avoided. May I read a passage from a book published recently by a young man who is attracting considerable attention? I am not saying he is an authority, but his writings are observed on the American continent at the present time. His name is Christopher Hollis, and the title of the book is The Breakdown of Money. He uses the following words, which ought to be impressive to all those who are seeking the causes of war. I read at page 93:
The Boer war, the Russo-Japanese war, the troubles in Egypt, on the further African coast, in the Balkans-all were terrible warnings of the inevitable nemesis of a world of exporting capitalists, each convinced that his

Corrupt Electoral Practices
money had a right to find its own level. Nineteen fourteen was the conclusion of the story.
Any party seeking the support of the people of Canada in an election at this time is invariably asked: What stand are you going to take on war? What are you doing about it? Are you committed to participation in a European war? Have you any entangling alliances with Great Britain? Hon. members know that is true. Why is this so? Because people are so completely bewildered with regard to the causes of war they are trying to the best of their ability to understand those causes and avoid them.

speechtext: I think the remarks of the hon. member are not being directed to the motion before the house. I would ask the hon. member to confine himself to the motion.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall endeavour to confine my remarks more closely to the subject before the house, although I think I could easily prove that these observations are strictly applicable to the causes of corruption in Canadian politics. But of course I submit to your ruling.
I hope you will permit me, sir, just to mention the other two principles of laissez-faire. One is free contracts, which would simply mean, for example, the abolition of trade unions. The other is metallic currency, which has been the cause of the most deplorable series of disasters which the human race has ever undergone. I shall leave the discussion of these until another time, but they bear most cogently upon the question we are discussing.
Now may I go on to show why these things have brought about this condition of corruption? There prevails a wide diversity of misconception. What do we mean by economic nationalism? Is it good or is it not? Is it the cause of war or is it not? There is general confusion in regard to the attitude on foreign relations. There are doubts as to the value of foreign trade, doubts as to the value of certain industries.
The Conservatives on the other hand are endeavouring to be true to their principles. I have not time to discuss that, and I gather from your opinion, Mr. Speaker, that it would be unwise for me to attempt to do so at any length. But I wish to show that the Conservatives also hardly know where they are at; nobody knows where he is at; nobody knows where either party is at. The result is that to come before the people and educate and train them so that they can think about real
issues instead of red herrings is to-day next to impossible.
The question then is, what are we going to do about it? I say that the cure for all this difficulty is the truth. Are the representatives of the parties that are in this house to-day, are the supporters of parties who are outside the house, willing to let the people know the truth and let the people judge and let the people rule? If the answer is yes, then it is indeed a simple matter for us to remove this outrageous blot of corruption. Let us in this parliament set to work an an earnest attempt to discover the truth; never mind playing politics, but find what is right, what is in the best interests of this country, what are the ideas which are advocated to-day and what are the points in favour of or against each of them. That is what should be done, without any confusing of the issue. Let me say that I greatly appreciate the attitude taken by hon. members of this house; I believe they are inclined to seek and follow the truth, although previous parliaments have been less inclined to do so. Very well; if we in this parliament are satisfied that it is the truth we want, that is the first point. Then are we willing to allow the truth to go over the radio-the truth and only the truth?

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: And in the press.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
And in the press, the truth and only the truth. Are we willing to have the bankers in the little branch banks in every community throughout this country know the truth and tell the truth, pure and unvarnished? If we are, it seems to me it is a proposal worthy of consideration that parliament should set aside for this purpose a sum of money before each election, on the principle that it is in the interests of this country that the people should know the truth; for a people who are uninformed, ignorant, deluded by misconceptions and false propaganda, are in an exceedingly dangerous state and are likely to do all sorts of unexpected and unaccountable and irresponsible things. Since, then, it is greatly in the interest of all concerned, and especially of governments, that the people should know the truth in the fullest possible degree, parliament should calmly and upon due consideration decide how much money may be necessary to permit the dissemination among the people of the various ideas entertained and put forward by the different political groups which seek election.
How much would it cost? We should set down a certain amount. Then suppose there
Corrupt Electoral Practices

are four parties facing the country at the next election, we say each of those parties shall be allowed a certain number of national hook-ups over the radio. Let each party have free speech over the radio, and let parliament pay for it; because parliament is interested in spreading the truth. There is grave danger, I say, in the people not having the truth; such a condition is likely to lead to communism, or fascism, or perhaps worse. Then, how much do the parties concerned require, within reasonable limits, to attend to stationery, advertising, pamphlets, letters and that kind of thing, all of which is necessary in conducting elections? Parliament will estimate the amount; it will set a figure, issue to the various parties the sums determined upon, and then allow them to go ahead and conduct their campaigns. Under that system the best party, according to the opinions of the people, would win.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: What about a new party just breaking in?

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Then, we must consider newspaper advertising. To a great degree this type of advertising enters into the campaigns in many constituencies. If that is thought advisable, money could be set aside for that purpose. In addition, there are halls to be engaged. If halls are necessary-and we all agree that they are-and if a certain number of meetings are to be held in the halls of a certain community, let us set aside certain moneys for those halls.
We must consider also transportation. At the present time there are very strict rules in connection with the transporting of people to the polls. So far as I have heard, it is well recognized that those rules are largely ignored. In my opinion that is a most unhealthy condition. If we are going to transport people to the polls, then let us make allowances for doing so. Let us have it attended to in an open and aboveboard manner.
If these things are done we would be prepared to approach the concerns the leader of the opposition has mentioned. He implied that there were organizations in the country which were making substantial contributions to election funds. I am going to assume-and I think it is only right that we should-that those organizations are making contributions because they want their particular ideas to prevail. Perhaps their ideas are the correct ones; who knows? If they are willing to contribute certain moneys in order to have their ideas prevail, why not allow them to make those contributions in an aboveboard
fMr. Blackmore.]
and open manner? Let the names of those who contributed be stated. Let the amounts be known. Let the purposes for which the contributions are made be stated. Let it be known whether it is the desire of the organization in question that the fund be allocated to the Conservative party. If it is so allocated, well and good. If it is given to the Liberal party, well and good.
That is the only way we have been able even to approach the solution of the problem in Alberta. Such having been done, we can now turn in this parliament to the task of determining the situation here. If investigations are made we will be able to go back, every one of us, and tell the truth, so far as we have been able to acquire it, and matters will be in a much healthier position when the next election comes along.
In this way we would be in a position whereby we might bring about a more enlightened Canada. I am satisfied about this, having lived in Alberta, where this thing has been done. There are plenty of people who are prepared to sneer at what has been done in Alberta, but the people who have been in the province, people who have been through those movements and know how an election is carried on out there, realize that the people's method is a great benefit. Improved practices tend to purify political life. I confess I can see no other way in which we can possibly purify and cleanse the public life of Canada, and in any way enable the people to register their will at any election.
Such being the case I take great pleasure in seconding the motion of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) that an investigation be conducted into the corrupt practice charges which have been made.

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the motion now before the house. First of all, as a member who has sat in his place for the last twelve years may I say here and now that I do not hold my seat through any kind of corruption or forced subscription of any kind to any corporation or interest.
I have read the words of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as they appear in Hansard, and I believe he said either too much or not enough. I must state sincerely that so far as I am personally concerned no strings are attached to my own activities. There has been no corruption in connection with my election, personally, and I believe this applies to all hon. members of the house.
To show how this matter may work out may I say that only a few days ago I received a request for a subscription to be made to one

Corrupt Electoral Practices
of the best Protestant churches in my part of the country, and I was only too pleased to subscribe. My only regret at the time was that I could not give more. I was in a position to know of the good work that church was doing for a large number of people in that pioneer section of my constituency.
Although the suggestion is made that democracy is at stake, I must say that it ill behooves members of parliament to make the statements which have been made to-day, and I think the atmosphere must be clarified. In this connection may I point out one or two things the Social Credit party has done in the province of Alberta, both provincially and federally. May I make reference at this time to the rash promises which were made in that province? Those were promises made by a party to gather the votes of the electors.
I vividly remember the first emergency session in 1930 when, for the first time, the previous parliament was assembled in Ottawa to deal with unemployment. I well remember that on that occasion the then prime minister, the present leader of the opposition, coming from the senate after hearing the speech from the throne, entered the door of the chamber behind Mr. Speaker's chair. Walking from that point to his seat in the house he received an ovation from every section of the House of Commons. But at the same time, walking with him, over and above him, were the promises he made during the previous campaign. Regardless of his work and regardless of the energy he exerted for his country from 1930 until 1935, the fact remains that those promises remained with him, so far as the electors of Canada were concerned, and the electors would not forget them.
The mover and the seconder of the amendment belong to the new Social Credit party. I have no personal grievance against that party. My sincere and earnest wish would be that from the activities of that party we might eventually find it possible to solve some of the great questions now confronting us and, if I may use the term, to humanize the monetary system of Canada and remove some of its anomalies. At the same time I must point out to hon. members of the Social Credit party how they won their election in Alberta, and also how the federal members attained their seats in this house. I well remember that some of the electors of that province sang the verses of that song:
We'll build a sweet little nest Somewhere in the west,
And let the rest of the world go by.
Social credit was going to solve all their problems. That was to be brought about through the politics of the Social Credit party
which were propounded to win the election. I say that it is the very worst kind of corruption for political parties to make promises that they know they cannot fulfil. I do not want to see any one party trying to outbid another in order to catch votes. I do not like to see them making appeals to the electorate and attempting to outbid one another in rash promises which could not possibly be implemented. I well remember that when the hon. member who formerly held the seat for Labelle, Mr. Bourassa, spoke some years ago he referred to the promises made by the then prime minister during the election campaign of 1930, and his statement was this: "Out of those promises will come one of two things; if you fulfil them you will bankrupt the country, and if you do not fulfil them you will go down in Canadian history as the greatest promiser the country has ever known."
What happened to the Social Credit party? I hold in my hand what is known as the Social Credit Manual in which is set out the system of social credit as applied to the province of Alberta and to all Canada. It purports to have been written by William Aber-hart, B.A., and was copyrighted in 1935. At page 14 of the manual we find a reference to basic dividends, and I quote:
To enable each citizen to secure these bare necessities, each of them will receive a pass book in which at the beginning of each month will be entered the basic dividend for that month, say $25.
If ever a corrupt appeal was made to the electors of a province or a country, certainly it was made right there by the Social Credit party. I am absolutely-

I w'ant hon. members to pay particular

That is the gospel and the policy that was spread, not only throughout Alberta but also throughout British Columbia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It did not get into the east, but I want to tell my hon. friends that the east has been very fair to the idea of social credit; we wanted to study it. We wanted to find a solution for some of the problems we were facing. I remember attending a meeting at the Chateau Laurier at which Major Douglas, the founder of social credit, made an address. I listened attentively and open-mindedly to what he bad to say and I hoped to find something useful in his formula. However, even with all his formulas I have never been able to find in them a solution for our social ills.
Major Douglas appeared before the banking committee of this house and again he brought forward his equations. We must be very careful about all these new economic equations brought forward by the theorists. Two and two does not make four according to them; it is much more complicated than that. You have figures on one side and then some letters and other symbols on the other, for the simplest questions. I was quite open-minded as far as Major Douglas was concerned, but for the life of me I never could plumb the abyss of social credit, and neither can the hon. members who have been elected on that policy.
A number of social crediters found it possible to be elected during the last dominion election. As far as they personally are concerned I have no doubt that they are a credit and an asset to our Canadian parliament, but we must remember that they were practically elected upon false promises and policies which they themselves found impossible of application when they were in power.

speechtext: Prove that statement.

speechtext: I ask the hon. member to withdraw that statement. I was elected by the people of Alberta not on false pretences, and I demand that that statement be withdrawn.

speechtext:
I say that hon. members were elected on- the promise of $25 per month to every adult in the province. The people of Alberta have given this provincial government all the leeway and latitude possible. Premier Aberhart has been given every opportunity to implement the promises

Corrupt Electoral Practices
he made and to demonstrate this wonderful new thing which was to take the people out of the depression, namely, social credit. At that time he was not worrying because he had asked the Albertans for eighteen months within which to implement these promises. That looked like a long time, but those eighteen months have elapsed and I do not think the social credit members as a group have been able to convince other hon. members of the wonderful benefits of social credit and that they have applied it to Alberta. I direct their attention to the old saying: Save yourself before you try to save anybody else.
Personally I have an open mind on these questions; I believe I would be remiss in my duty as a member of this house if I said that everything was all right and that we had no difficulties to surmount as far as the economic and financial situation is concerned. But there are serious problems which we have to face, and this is not tfie time when a political party should be prostituting itself by making irrational and passionate appeals to the people in the form of bribes.
I have been informed by good authority as to just what went on during the last provincial and federal elections. The social credit candidate would be addressing an audience in the rural section of the province. Naturally there would be some married women in the audience. The speaker would turn to a married woman and ask her if she were satisfied. She might reply that she was, that she had a good husband. He would then ask her, " Have you all the money you want?" The answer would be, " No, my husband is poor." Then the candidate would say, " If you vote for us we will give you $25 a month for your own money." If that was not the worst kind of bribery, I do not know what it was.
Then a social credit candidate would be addressing a group of young girls, no doubt most of whom were thinking of marrying- after all, that would be quite logical. They would be asked, " Have you all the money you want? Would you not like to have a nice hat or a nice pair of shoes?" The reply would be, " Yes, but I have not the money." Then the statement would be made, "Vote for us and we will give you $25 a month." Again I say that that was the worst possible kind of bribery.
I repeat what I said at the beginning. I believe in a hundred per cent confederation. What we want is purity as far as politics are concerned. Party funds there are, and there is no need to blush for that. I give to my own church and to other churches. That is not a fault; I am still loyal to my own
church, but I also know of good work done by other's. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that there is no stigma attaching to any member of this parliament, no matter on which side of the house he sits, in connection with party funds. But if corruption were rampant I would be the first one to hold up both hands for the amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) upon his courage in bringing this resolution before the house. I think it is unfortunate that so far, since his speech, the debate has tended to become a purely party affair.

But I would like to bring the house back, if I may, to the resolution now before it.
No one can sit in this house as I have done for some sixteen years without hearing a good many charges of political corruption. No one can go through a number of campaigns east and west without being fairly sure that vast sums of money are being spent in elections. Further than that, under the present elections act we have no means of ascertaining whence these large sums come. Some years ago when that act was being revised some of us tried to have inserted an amendment under which we would have a record of the sums given by local people and also the sums given to the central campaign funds, but the government would not accept an amendment along that line.
It is only a few days ago, as the hon. member for Peace River has pointed out, that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made some very serious statements. It is true he did not make any very definite charges, but he made some very serious statements. I would point out to the house that he is in a somewhat different position from that occupied by the ordinary member of the house. He is a recognized official of the house, and when he
Corrupt Electoral Practices

makes a charge in the house it cannot lightly be set aside. As has been said by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), he said either too much or too little. The impression that there is something radically wrong in the conduct of elections has gone abroad from one end of this dominion to the other. I recognize that even though this matter should be referred to a committee, it might be very difficult to secure all the evidence desired. I presume members of the government may say that they are not going to allow us to set up a committee that might go on a fishing expedition or something of the kind. I know there are limitations to the work a committee can accomplish. At the same time I feel that it is in the interests of clean government in this country that charges of this kind should not be allowed to pass unchallenged. Unless democracy can work in an atmosphere of something like reasonable freedom, democracy becomes a veritable sham. An impression is abroad throughout the country that to-day it is money that rules in elections as in a good many other fields. I think, Mr. Speaker, that when charges as serious as this, even though they are not specific, are made, they should be investigated by this house. I have therefore very great pleasure in supporting the motion of the hon. member for Peace River.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Woodsworth) expressed regret that the discussion which has taken place this afternoon should have partaken of a partisan nature. If he had that regret I must say I wish he had been wise enough to advise those around him as to the consequences of bringing in the motion on the subject to which it relates in the form in which it is. Just an hour or so ago I moved that the house resolve itself into committee of supply in order that the government might obtain the wherewithal to carry on the business of government. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) has moved an amendment to that motion, which is to the effect that the house shall not go into supply but shall do something else. What that something else is I shall remind 
the house in a few moments. But what would be the effect of the amendment were it to be carried? The effect would simply be that the government would be defeated, no supply could be voted and there matters would end for a time at least. It is a motion of want of confidence in the administration, and as such it is necessary that the administration oppose it so as to make possible its right to govern in this country, with the loyal support of its following in this house.
Had hon. gentlemen opposite desired a discussion in a manner which would not involve a vote of a want of confidence, there being no charge of any kind against the administration, they might have given notice of a motion in the regular way upon which the subject matter of the resolution might have been fully discussed. There would then have been perfect freedom on the part of all to discuss the matter regardless of their relationship to the government or otherwise. It is necessary, however, for me to point out clearly that the motion in the form in which it has been presented is a want of confidence motion in the administration, and if it were to carry, the government would be defeated. It is a want of confidence motion based on what? On nothing whatever in the way of substance.
May I remind the house what the hon. member said about his own amendment? I shall read the amendment first:
This house is of the opinion that charges of levies in connection with Canadian National Railways contracts as 'well as statements concerning electoral corruption should be referred to a select committee of this house with power to send for papers, persons and witnesses and to take evidence under oath and to report to this house.
After he had read his motion, he asked over and over again: Is it not desirable that we should remove these shadows which are on the horizon? Is it not necessary that we should remove the shadow which is over this house? Is it not necessary that we should do away with the stigma that has been placed upon this parliament? Are we not here for the purpose of preserving the honour of this parliament, of saving it from dishonour? Let me ask my hon. friends who have spoken on the other side of this house: Who have created this shadow? Who have spoken words which have cast reflection upon this parliament, other than the hon. member who moved this resolution, the hon. member who seconded it, and I regret to say also, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett)? It is a new alliance that we have, this Conservative-Social Credit alliance, which has

taken also into its fold the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth). These gentlemen have been spending their time since this parliament opened to see how far they can go in manufacturing shadows-

maintopic: CORRUPT ELECTORAL PRACTICES-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
There is not a member of this house-neither the leader of the opposition, the mover of the amendment, the seconder of the amendment, nor the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group-who has had the courage to stand up in this house and say that he has a specific charge to make against any member of the government or of this house or against any one of those who have been carrying on the public business of this country. I say that, until a specific charge is made, the duty of this parliament is to go on with its regular work and not permit itself to be diverted from the business of the country by shadows which are the creation of minds too full of darkness to bring forth the truth they talk so much about.
What is the kind of language which we have been obliged to listen to this afternoon? Let me refer to what we heard from the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who seconded the amendment. He talked about an octopus-about some general feeling throughout Canada that somewhere or other there was an octopus whose long, hidden, treacherous tentacles were clandestinely getting a grip on the whole country. I wonder if that is patriotic language? I wonder if that is language calculated to create pride and esteem in the breasts of young Canadians, who he says need good examples in all these matters. The effort to besmirch parliament and to dishonour the names of men in public life is to my mind the most contemptible of all possible actions. I say that hon. members who have nothing specific in the way of charges to bring before this house had better remain silent when it comes to seeking to discredit others thereby maligning the institution of which they themselves happen to be members.
My hon. friend who moved this amendment said that when I spoke previously with regard to the subject matter of electoral corruption I read a prepared statement. He emphasized two or three times that the statement was a prepared one. It was prepared, and designedly so, and for the reason that I am going to give my hon. friend. Had I made a statement of my own my hon. friend might have been the first to say, "We are listening to the Prime Minister making his own statement on this matter. We know that he is concerned in these matters, and we therefore ask you to take his statement with a grain of salt." I requested the clerk of this house to give me a statement as to the procedure which the parliament of Canada, and in particular the House of Commons, should adopt with respect to any charges of electoral corruption, a statement that I might read to all hon. members, setting forth the position beyond possibility of contradiction or controversy. I then read to this house what the laws of this country, the laws of this parliament, have set forth as the method of dealing with questions of this kind, and referred to the rules and regulations of the House of Commons in dealing with such matters.
This is not the first time in the history of Canada that vague and general charges of electoral corruption have been made. They have been made ever since there has been a parliament, and they will continue to be made as long as we have men who are prepared to besmirch the institutions with which they are associated. In order to protect 'honourable men who wish to keep themselves free from that kind of thing, parliament has enacted laws to protect its members. They are a part of the laws of the country to-day. They prescribe the methods which must be followed in dealing with questions of this kind. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) says he does not care anything about laws; he is not interested in them. Well, we are. There are far too many people in this country to-day who are asserting the very doctrine which my hon. friend has asserted, that they do not care anything about laws, that they are not going to be governed by laws. It is just that kind of thing that this government is going to stop, if we can possibly do it, and regain in our country a proper respect for law. The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), who spoke a few moments ago, properly pointed out that those who adopt this tone have not only forgotten respect for law but have forgotten respect for fair and honourable methods of procedure, to an extent which a few years ago would not have been countenanced for one minute. Never before
Corrupt Electoral Practices

in the history of Canada, until it was done by the party to which my hon. friend who moved this resolution belongs, did an]' party come forward and openly offer to pay five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five dollars a month to those whose support it sought; nothing of that kind ever occurred before in the history of this dominion. And if we are gradually slipping down to a point where we are beginning to talk about corruption from one end of Canada to the other, and an octopus which has its tentacles all over this country, it is due to that very corrupting of the electorate in a manner and to a degree such as this country has never known heretofore.
Let me say to my hon. friends that if the laws are not adequate to deal with the question of corruption in electoral campaigns or of corruption in any other place, or way, or form, if there are hon. members who can bring forward suggestions which will make our laws better than they are, the present administration will be only too willing to work with them to the full to give such suggestions, if they are at all workable, a place on our statutes. We are only too anxious to see that our electoral laws are made as effective as possible to prevent anything in the nature of corruption. The government intends, in pursuance of its promise at the last session, to deal with the franchise and with the electoral laws again this year, so there will be an opportunity for all hon. members to come forward with any suggestions which they may have, any concrete, practical proposals which they may care to make. The government will be glad to consider any such proposals. I here and now invite hon. members, instead of wasting their time in doing what they can to defame the institution of parliament and democratic government in this country, to come along with practical suggestions whereby we can prevent in the future anything of the kind which they to-day are imagining has taken place in the past, or which actually may have taken place in the past.
What then is the method of proceeding with matters of this kind? It is well known. If anyone has a charge to make, let him make it as a specific charge, not in the form of a general allegation. What does the amendment say?
This house is of the opinion that charges of levies in connection with Canadian National Railways contracts as well as statements concerning electoral corruption should be referred to a select committee of this house-
Since when have we begun to refer statements on different matters to special committees of this house? We would have

time for nothing else were we to start that sort of thing. The hon. gentleman refers to charges of levies in connection with the Canadian National Railways. Where and by whom have the charges been made? Did the leader of the opposition make a charge? Not a bit of it. He made a general statement. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests that the position of the leader of the opposition is one of exceptional significance and importance in this house. It is, and for that very reason my right hon. friend should have been the first to see that no general allegations fell from his lips, but that a specific statement was made in the nature of a charge if he wished to have the subject investigated. May I say to the right hon. gentleman and to every member of this house here and now that if he or any hon. member will make a specific charge with respect to corruption and will say that he has reasonable ground for believing that he can bring forward evidence to substantiate that charge, this government will give him a committee immediately to have the charge investigated. I say that not only to the leader of the opposition but to every member of this house; and further, I say that until hon. members are prepared to make specific charges they should cease to make allegations which they are not brave enough to back up or have not sufficient knowledge to substantiate in any shape or form.
We are not here as a government to fight shadows. My hon. friend says, "Let us remove these shadows on the horizon; let us remove the shadow which overclouds this house." I say, give us something of substance and we will have it investigated; but we will not spend our time fighting shadows conjured up by hon. gentlemen opposite.
And now may I mention one other matter- probably it was an oversight on the part of the hon. member for Peace River. There are certain customs which are well understood with respect to the conduct of business in this house, customs which enable debate to proceed with more in the way of information than would otherwise be possible for those participating. One of these customs is that where an amendment is to>
be moved on going into supply the administration should be given some notice of it, so that at least there may be an opportunity, when the house .is considering the question, to have citations and references specifically quoted, that statements made in the course of debate may be substantiated. The hon. member has moved this amendment without saying a word to the government in advance about his intentions

in the matter. I happened to hear a rumour that the leader of the opposition had been talking last night in the corridor with the hon. member who seconded the amendment, and they were heard to say that the hon. member for Peace River would bring something forward to-day Knowing pretty well what that something might be, I assumed that this was the kind of motion we were likely to have from him. In the few hurried moments at my disposal I sought to recall incidents in this house in previous years when the Conservative party, while in opposition, and usually beginning at the third session of parliament, started something in the nature of scandal. I therefore looked up Hansard to find out what took place during one of the sessions when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was prime minister and I found in the third session of the tenth parliament the record of exactly the same sort of thing that we have at the present moment. Everything was brought forward in much the same way. The stage was set in the first instance by having someone come along with a general charge, a general statement alleging among other things graft on the part of some ministers of the crown. That is the kind of thing that is meant by levies on the Canadian National Railways-talk of graft. At that time the very same comment was made that fell from the lips of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) the other evening-that the hon. gentleman making the general statement had said either too much or too little-and the then member for Labelle, who was sensitive in these matters of political honour, moved in this house one day that either what had been said should be put in the form of a substantial charge or that the words should be withdrawn. I had expected that this would be the form of motion that we should have had from my hon. friend to-day, namely, that either a substantial charge should be made or that the words should be withdrawn. But he has not put his motion in that form. He has gone a step farther, and as if a charge had already been made has asked that a committee be appointed immediately to investigate the matter.
Let me draw my hon. friend's attention to what was said on the occasion to which I [DOT]have referred. I am not going to mention the names of those who participated, those who at the time had to do with general charges. I do not think it reflected credit upon them then, and now that they are gone I do not wish to discredit their names further. The
statement was made by one hon. member that he was going to discuss certain things including graft. Then the hon. member stated further, pretty much as the leader of the opposition has done on this occasion, that he had "data" and "material" at his disposal with respect to charges. The motion that was presented to the chair by the then member for Labelle was:
That such a statement, undefined as it is, with regard to the parties concerned, reflects on the honour of the house and of the government;
That the hon. member be therefore invited, either to name the ministers and members of the house to whom he was referring-*
On such-and-such a date.
-and to specify his charges against them, or to withdraw his accusation.
That unless the hon. member complies with that request and adopts one of these two courses, he stands censured by this house.
The matter had been pretty fully discussed on a previous occasion and His Honour the Speaker was obliged, because of the previous discussion, to rule that it could not be discussed again and for that reason the Speaker ruled the motion out of order, and was sustained in his ruling when it was challenged. But the purpose of the motion was to clear the record as quickly as possible of any imputation in the one way in which parliament where a specific charge is made has always dealt with such matters.
I wish now to read to the house what Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking in this house with respect to that motion, had to say about the method to be adopted in dealing with general questions of political corruption, graft and the like.

Sir Wilfrid Laurier said;
If the object of the hon. member for Labelle is to clear the atmosphere of the house, there are eases and cases showing how this is to be done. The house has affirmed, and it is also the rule of the house which has come to us from the mother of parliaments, that the conduct or standing of any member of this house cannot be impugned except upon cause being shown and until a member rises in his place in the house and says: I have reason to believe and I can prove such and such a thing against a member. If, at a later period, the hon. member for Labelle or anybody else thinks there is in this house any member who ought not to be a member of it, who has disgraced himself, or whose conduct ought to be investigated, it is open to him to demand such an investigation, but the house, I hope, will not depart from the sound traditions which

country coming from two directions, supposed to be opposed to each other but having much in common-

speechtext: No, not the Liberal and Conservative parties, but the communist and fascist parties, each of which desires to do away with the parliamentary system of political parties having free discussion on the floor of parliament and to substitute for it dictatorship. And the method which they are adopting to bring this about is to besmirch as much as they can the institution of parliament, and the names of men in public life, to make general charges, insinuations, allegations and the like, with a view to creating from end to end of the country the impression that democratic institutions have failed and that they with their dictatorships should take their place. I have given some little
attention to that problem, and have considered how it might be dealt with. In England and in Australia they have seen fit to put limitations upon amounts which might be expended. In Australia, where they had much the same conditions as we have talked about, this afternoon, they also impose compulsory voting, so as to lessen improper expenditure.
I know, too, our statute provides that if a member who has not made returns takes his seat in the house, he is liable to a penalty of $500 a day. There is at least one hon. member who has sat here and who has voted, but who, according to the report of the returning officer, has made no return. What are we going

Corrupt Electoral Practices,
to do about a situation of that kind? Well, somebody would have to bring action against him, and thereby incur the odium of bringing such action. Can we not deal with it in some other way?
When the elections act comes before the house for consideration I propose to offer certain observations and to make certain suggestions with respect to amendments, by which we may endeavour to cure the conditions to which I have referred, for it is a canker eating at the very life of the country. We all know that England went through that period. Hon. members will recall that history credits Walpole with saying that every man had his price. Hon. members will recall how the matter was dealt with. It was a long time, in England, before they attained to that excellence in the conduct of elections which now prevails in that country. Has anyone who has any interest in the expenditure of public moneys taken the trouble to ascertain where the money came from which was provided in the recent by-elections? Where did it come from? Did it come off the trees? Did it come out of the air? Who put it up, and why?
These are questions which come up periodically. It was to a matter of that kind to which I was directing attention the other day when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) interrupted me and stated that he had to do with a number of contracts for the Canadian National Railways, and stated that he knew nothing of this. Well, I did not suggest that he did. He suggests that he had no knowledge of it. Well, will my worst critic say or suggest that I said he had? What I did say, in answer to his statement, was that I was prepared to show that levies were being made on contractors- and that is an entirely different matter. It has not to do with the honour of the house. It has not to do with the respectability of individuals, unless you bring home to them the knowledge of it.
I have no reason for suggesting that the Minister of Transport had any knowledge of such a condition, and I have not said that he had such knowledge. An effort has been made to make it appear that what I said was that individuals were responsible for this. That is not what I said, nor was it inferred. What I did say was that those who were in charge of the raising of campaign funds were getting funds in that way. We do not have to leave this city, apparently, to find it out. I am sure there is not within sound of my voice a member who, if he takes the trouble
to inquire, will not find that those who sell goods or have contracts are being asked for contributions. I said the other day that I am not hypocrite enough for a single minute to deny that contributions are made to the campaign funds of political parties. Of course they are, and we all know they are. What is more, this is done very often with the best of motives.
Sir Joseph Flavelle has said that he had contributed to political parties from his youth. When he earned his first dollar his mother suggested that part of it should go to the church and part to his party. He said that the Right Hon. Mackenzie King was assisted by his contributions when he was running in Waterloo. He made that clear in the public statement he made the other day when addressing the shareholders of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. He said, "Although I think I am a Tory"-I do not know whether he used the word "Tory"-"I did that."
I happen to know that one of the leading contributors to the Liberal party, now no more, said that he believed it was quite proper that rich men should make contributions in order to enable those who were not of their political faith to be able to live in the communities decently and maintain their positions. As a matter of fact that gentleman was one of the contributors to the Asquith fund. What is more, if the right hon. gentleman would only take the trouble to think for a moment he would realize that there are presents and gifts made to men who are not regarded as being in favourable financial circumstances to enable them to maintain their position. Hon. members know that quite often purses are presented to public men. Personally I think that is wrong, but it is done. Reference was made to that on one occasion in the house.
That is the point I was endeavouring to make the other day. I repeat it and I withdraw no word of what I said. It must follow that there are hon. members who know just as well as I that their friends are making contributions to political campaign funds. I was making clear the difference which exists between the contribution that a man makes and an enforced contribution, which I said was a levy. If I say to a contractor, "You have to pay ten per cent, or even one per cent," I am putting him in a position which I think is manifestly unfair. For instance, if you have men who do business with the departments and who are entitled to sums of money, whether for rebates or for refunds of overpaid customs duties or otherwise, it is neither right

There are men from western Canada who know what happened. What is more, there are people who were made bankrupt and ruined financially because of the outcome of those very transactions. All this is known. Every time I hear people talk about irrigation in western Canada I realize, as most men do, what happened in that connection.
I wonder why it is that we are unwilling to spend a little time in going over the

political history of our country. Many members of the house know-I do not say all of them-that they are assisted in the conduct of their elections from some central fund. More than that, they know that that fund is collected by somebody before the election takes place. I remember one of the leading ministers on the Liberal side saying to me in a personal conversation that the difficulty about holding an election at that particular time was the fact that they had no money. Those who take the time to read the speech of the Prime Minister in connection with the Beauharnois scandal and the valley of humiliation will understand fully what I mean. He pointed out the difficulty in the conduct of parties and elections and organizations without money.
Those are the facts to which I was directing and to w'hich I still direct attention. If these matters affected this house alone, the problem would be simpler, but I was also dealing with provincial matters over which this house would have no jurisdiction. That is the reason why I did not endeavour in any sense to specify particular transactions to which reference could be made. Those are matters with which the provinces themselves must deal. This house will have before it the elections act and I trust that an endeavour will be made so to safeguard the sanctity of the franchise as not to allow corrupt forces and influences to prevent the free and untrammelled will of the people from being expressed at the polls. That is the purpose which I had in mind when I directed attention to the matter.
I am not greatly concerned, at my age, about many things. I have seen, I have known, I have encountered the accumulated money of my opponents to defeat me, and what is more I have seen it used on a tremendous scale with respect to one matter only that I shall mention, and that was when Alberta was not allowed to have its own natural resources. All one has to do is to look at the records of those days and one has a very clear appreciation of the situation. I speak whereof I know with respect to these matters, and I say the time has come when we must endeavour to the best of our ability to provide ways and means that will at least do something to curb these scandalous practices.
The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) complained very bitterly because one of the members of this chamber said that corruption was like an octopus. The right hon. gentleman said that it was a bad thing for the people of this country to have to
listen to the idea that the money power was thus powerful. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister himself said that the struggle of this parliament must be a struggle against the money power. Those are not my words; they are his. That is not my statement; it is his. He said this parliament must grapple and fight with the money power. And so, when a member says that corruption is an octopus which fastens its tentacles upon the body politic and destroys it, the simple question is, is it true? That is the issue.
There is one thing more. The right hon. gentleman spoke of the dangers that threaten the body politic from communism, on the one hand, and from fascism on the other. My recollection is that he found the chief fascist in the world, Herr Hitler, a most entertaining person and a man who is doing great work.
