Yes, it makes a lot of difference where we sit, and the right hon. gentleman who sits to the right of the Speaker to-day as Prime Minister finds the situation entirely different from what he did when he sat to the left. Then everything was wrong; everything was black; everything that was done by those in office in those strenuous days merited only criticism, abuse and vilification. But now, clothed with power, sitting in the seats of the mighty, hon. gentlemen on the government side by a stroke of the pen pass an order in council that destroys the wheat board-and all is well in Israel! We took other steps, to which reference will be made as the session proceeds, to accomplish similar ends. But now, because attention is directed to one thing that does merit the condemnation of every thoughtful Canadian, young or old, rich or poor, you are besmirching the honour of the house-when no reference was made to any member of this house! Reference was made to a member of the other chamber but that had nothing to do with this particular chamber.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that while this motion is not in my judgment the correct method by which to approach the problem which the member for Peace River desires to deal with, nevertheless the methods indicated by the Prime Minister the other day with respect to controverted elections and matters of that sort do not exhaust the powers of this house to deal with the problem, and when the electoral law is up for revision, as it will be, we can at least expect that the Prime Minister and his government will, with every member of the house, see to it that every possible provision is made to prevent these evils from continuing in Canada. The experience of other countries cries aloud to us.
There is no question of shadows. I was not dealing with shadows; I was dealing with realities, and very real things too. I was dealing with actualities, and, as I said the other day, instances could be multiplied if one so desired. But that has to do with something which is outside this chamber. It has to do with an individual and the methods he pursues in doing certain things. No one complains that he, as leading member of an organization committee, should do certain things. But the methods pursued we have a

right to criticize, and we do; everything that I said on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I repeat, and I say that if the government take any offence at what I have said they have it within their power to adopt that resolution and deal with it.

speechtext:
Mr. WILFRID LACROIX (Quebec-Mon-t-moremcy) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Civil Service Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of the bill is to provide th'at no person already belonging to the civil service in a province, and unable to speak French, may be transferred, in either a permanent or a temporary capacity, to the province of Quebec. I know that necessities of administration sometimes compel a minister to appoint to positions in the province of Quebec under his department, officials who, while fully competent in other respects, do not speak the language of the majority of people in that province.
From the moment of their arrival in Quebec, such officials necessarily come in contact with the French speaking public, and their inability to speak the language of the people with whom they have to deal sometimes gives rise to annoyances sufficient to create the impression that Quebec is not treated as it should be, and to bring about in the long run the very thing every hon. member wishes to avoid, namely conflicts detrimental to Canadian unity.
Without attaching any -blame to any of the departments concerned, which evidently select for such positions the officials at their disposal, I am confident that by amending the act in the manner indicated in the bill it would be possible to create a staff capable of
speaking French with ease and fluency. There would thus be opened to our bilingual young men positions which, so far, they have had difficulty in obtaining.
The officials I have in mind, those who speak only English, passed their civil service examinations in an outside province and, on being transferred to Quebec, were not subjected to any further test. I suggest that in such cases further examinations be held, and that officials appointed to positions in Quebec be required to prove their ability to understand the people of that province, and to be understood by them. Not only is this fair, but it would work out to the -advantage of the service.
It is principally the officials of the Department of Agriculture sent to Quebec as inspectors of live stock or farm products who find themselves in contact with a population almost entirely composed of people speaking the French language. May I add that outside the civil service mistakes of that kind are also made. Even in the ancient city of Champlain, which is certainly the most French of all cities in America there is an engineer in charge of all national defence undertakings who cannot speak a word of French.
I acknowledge with pleasure the good will shown by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in connection with the emr ployment of French speaking officials; but to every complaint I have made to him he has -eplied, through his deputy minister, that he had at his disposal no engineer who could speak French.	.
I am fully convinced that if the act contained a section compelling every official called upon to serve in Quebec to prove, through examination, his knowledge of the French language, this would be a step towards that unity which is so greatly needed to-day. Moreover it would give to those -people in my province who possess the required qualifications an opportunity to obtain these positions. One can scarcely conceive of a French Canadian official unable to make himself understood in- English being transferred to Toronto or Kingston. His stay in either place would surely be a short one.
I do not wish to make a lengthy speech; still less do I wish to raise the racial cry. I request simply that my province be placed on the same footing as the other provinces. Firmly convinced of the justice of my cause, I am content to rely upon the broad-mindedness of hon. members for the passage of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think I would fail to discharge properly my duties were I not to express approval of the amendment to the Civil Service Act proposed by the hon. member for Quebec Montmorency (Mr. Lacroix). To my mind the amendment is based on justice and common sense. During the first session of this parliament I made the following statement:
A certain discontent seems to exist in the province of Quebec regarding the number of positions held by French speaking Canadians in the federal service.
In support of that statement I gave certain statistics which may be found on page 2720 of Hansard of 1936. Since I made that statement conditions have not materially changed or improved.
What I am about to say I intend to say in a frank and candid manner. My criticism is not against the government; it is against the actual system and possibly indirectly against those who apply the system. Throughout the province of Quebec there is a feeling that federal civil service positions are not awarded in the correct proportion to French and English speaking Canadians. I am quite prepared to admit that considerable misapprehension exists as to the power and jurisdiction of the commission. I shall even go so far as to say that many people, unfortunately too many, still have the impression that members of the House of Commons or ministers of the government have the final say in recommending and designating who, among several candidates for a civil service position, shall have the appointment. This is not the case. I know that the commission has the first and last say in the matter of making appointments. If that is not the fact I should like someone to tell me.
I should like to cite one instance which occurred in Cap de la Madeleine. About two years ago the civil service commission invited applications by bilingual candidates for the position of caretaker for a post office building which had just been erected. That town has
a population of about 10,000, and I doubt if one half of one per cent of the people are English speaking. This caretaker would not have to speak English more than once in ten years in the carrying out of his duties, unless he took the notion once in a while to go down in the basement and address himself to the Scotch anthracite coal pile. It took the commission about a year to realize the true situation, and then new applications were invited. This happened six months ago, but as yet the examination has not been held nor has the date been announced. No doubt it will take another six months to close this matter finally. The result is that it has taken over two years to fill the position of caretaker in a post office. There are many candidates for this position and I may say they are all exasperated at the delay.
Many people throughout the country are dissatisfied with the commission. I know many members of the House of Commons are dissatisfied, and I would not be surprised to hear that some ministers are not totally satisfied. This feeling is regrettable, but it has existed for a number of years. The sooner the system is either changed or improved, the better it will be for all concerned. After all, the commission should not be looked upon as being an absolutely permanent and unchangeable fixture. It should not be considered as a bureaucracy.
Reverting to the dissatisfaction and misapprehension that exist in connection with the work of this commission, I want to say most emphatically that the one factor which has contributed the most to creating this dissatisfaction and misapprehension is the appointment by the commission of persons to certain positions who can hardly speak the language of those with whom they would come in daily contact in the fulfilment of their official duties. That such a state of affairs has existed in the province of Quebec is not to be doubted. These things will happen again unless the law is changed, as suggested by the hon. member for Quebec Montmorency, and it will be to the detriment of those good relations which should exist between French and English populations in this country. I name no one. I have no personal animosity against those who are holding positions in the civil service which they are not fit to hold. My sole and sincere desire is to do away with such unwise, unfit, and I will say, unfair nominations.
The present amendment will serve the purpose in view. Candidates who seek a bilingual position ought to submit to a bilingual exam-

ination, and moreover, the bilingual test should be one of the most important items of the examination. I repeat that one who cannot speak the language of those with whom he is bound to act naturally cannot understand their mentality or customs, and he cannot but be a failure and a cause of friction. I venture to say that if there is dissatisfaction and suspicion in the province of Quebec in regard to the civil service commission, it is due to the fact that some people have been appointed to positions who could not satisfactorily fill them because they could not speak the language or understand the mentality of the people with whom they had to deal.
Some may suggest this grudge seems to exist only in Quebec. It may possibly be so, but to those who find it strange or singular that the grudge or dissatisfaction should be limited to that province I would say that they are not acquainted with the facts or aware of what is taking place in Quebec. Those people who so wonder would appreciate the circumstances better if the situation were reversed. Suppose a man from the province of Quebec who could hardly speak English, and knew little about the mentality or customs of the English speaking people of this country, were appointed to a civil service position where he had to deal with people in the city of Toronto, for example, or Calgary or some other English speaking city. I wonder what the people there would say of such an appointment. I am sure they would have reason to be dissatisfied and to have a grudge against the system that permitted such appointments. How long would they stand for it? I do not say that the people of Toronto are not as fair-minded as the people of any other city, and I am sure they would not stand very long for a man holding a civil service position who could not speak the language which is generally spoken in that city.
In the province of Quebec, not all the people-for I do not want to exaggerate-but some people, too many people, in fact, feel that they have generously, and with resignation and self-denial for the sake of peace and harmony, stood for such appointments until their patience is exhausted. This is not a threat; it is rather a warning and a statement of facts. It is a statement of a most unfortunate reality. The proposed amendment to the Civil Service Act will remedy this grievance, and I therefore most heartily support it because I think it will remove one of the causes of unrest in my province.

I am far from endeavouring to discuss the details of the amendment, which, I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will at once see, will have the effect of restricting rather than enlarging the opportunities, because they would segregate each province as such, instead of carrying out what has been so long in the minds both of parliament and of the commission, that those who serve communities in which both the English and French languages are used should have knowledge of both these languages to enable them properly and adequately to discharge their duties. There have been many difficulties; I know of them; but I can say I do not believe that at any time there has been a deliberate effort on the part of either the civil service commission on the one hand or ministers on the other to prevent, either directly or indirectly, those who are appointed to the public service from communicating with the community they serve in the language of the majority of that community. If it were so, the sooner it is stopped the better, because it is desirable that the men who occupy these positions should be able to communicate with those who are affected by the service rendered, in either the French or English language, they being the two languages which are officially recognized in this country.
I make these observations from some knowledge and experience with respect to the matter, and with the earnest desire to see the principle for which the hon. gentlemen are^contending given effect to, but not, in my judgment, by the legislation now before the house, which in detail, I repeat-and I think the Minister of Justice will, upon examination, agree-effects a restrictive principle, rather than enlarges the opportunities for those who will be served. If it were referred to a committee, the Civil Service Commission, I feel satisfied, would be able to arrive at a solution that would meet the difficulties to which the hon. gentleman has referred and which, in my judgment, should be remedied at the earliest possible date.

speechtext:
I desire to say only a few words
on this bill, as evidently, from the remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and my own, it will be found that both sides of the house are practically in agreement on the principle involved. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lacroix) upon the very able way in which he has presented this bill;
I would also express my congratulations to the leader of the opposition for the short but illuminative remarks that he has made about the bill.
This question has arisen in the past in many ways, both inside and outside the house, and I might say that there has been an effort to find a solution to the problem, although in practice it evidently has not reached its full expression. May I point out in the first place that already there is in the Civil Service Act a section which to a certain degree touches on this point. Section 32 of the act provides that:
Every examination under this act shall be held in the English or French language, at the option of the candidate; and notice of every examination shall be published in the English and French languages in the Canada Gazette, and such notice shall state the number of positions that it is expected will be open for appointments, the positions that are then vacant, and in each case the qualifications required for such positions.
It has been the practice in a number of cases in advertising positions to state whether the two languages are required, or whether only one of the languages is necessary. As regards transfers, section 21, subsection 3 of the act provides:
Except as to appointments to positions in the headquarters of the several departments and other portions of the civil service at Ottawa, the appointments to any local positions in any province shall, so far as practicable, be made from persons having resided in such localities for a period of at least one year immediately preceding the date last fixed for receiving applications for such local positions.
And in the civil service regulations, section 54 further provides:
In recommending a transfer in which a change of residence is involved, the deputy head of the department in which the vacancy exists must certify that the position in question cannot be filled efficiently by local promotion, or must advance sufficient reasons for his recommendation to satisfy the commission that in this particular instance it is in the best interests of the public service that transfer should supersede promotion.
It will be seen from these quotations that in the Civil Service Act and in the regulations of the commission some attention has already been given to the language question and also reservations have been made to make as much as possible the transfer from one province into another exceptional cases. I might quote also, but it would delay the discussion, passages from the annual report of the civil service commission, 1934, where this commission deals with this matter and points out certain of the things that I myself have indicated this evening. But apparently these

I think we all agree that this is undesirable. To that extent, I believe, the house should be unanimous in accepting the principle involved in this bill.
But I have some sympathy with the remarks made by the leader of the opposition as to the exact wording of the sections proposed as amendments. In the first place, I think that although the language question should be primary, it is desirable that the amendments should not. be made stringent to a point where they might prevent either the commission or whoever is in charge of the appointment from giving consideration to other qualifications which may be required in exceptional appointments where a scientist or other technical man or a person of special experience may be needed. In the second place I am not sure that by making the province the territorial limit within which this bill is supposed to act, there is not a danger that in certain instances we may arrive at the opposite goal to the one we wish to attain. speechtext:
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the criminal code.
He said: As I intimated when I introduced this bill, its purpose is:
-to prevent employers from refusing to employ, or from dismissing employees, or conspiring with others therefor, for the reason that they are members of a trade union.
As it is lawful for workmen or employees to form themselves into trade unions and to bargain collectively, it should, as a matter of public policy, be unlawful for employers to seek by overt acts or intimidation, threats or conspiracy to prevent them from belonging to such trade unions.
The right of labour to organize is recognized by the treaty of peace. I quote:
The right of association for all lawful purposes by the employed as well as by the employers.
Section 497 of the criminal code distinctly exempts trade unions from the class of unlawful organizations: notwithstanding that, it is extremely difficult in practice for trade unions to carry forward their organization work. As an example of the arrogant attitude of employers I might quote what was said by some of them during the investigation by the textile commission. The president of one company said:
The men can belong to any union if they like. We do not ask a man if he belongs to a union or what his religion may be, but the board of directors refuse to recognize the union, any union.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
The president of another company said:
I never had to deal with a union here before, never heard of such a thing, and I am not going to be led by a lot of such folk as if I might just have a rope around my neck and be led like a lamb to the slaughter.
Another manager said:
We have no objection whatever to our employees joining any kind of organization they feel so disposed to. I don't think we would be prepared to consider dealing with any organization. Because we would very much prefer to deal with them as individuals. Because there are always people who get in control of these things, or it seems to be the case, who have very radical ideas, imaginary ills or problems.
And yet another:
The company will not permit any third party to interfere between the management and the employees or to take away from the employees their rights as individuals to deal with the company.
I wish to give one honourable exception. The president of one particular company made this statement:
We as manufacturers ... we have got the right to organize ourselves. Isn't it right that labour should have the same right?
That is all that I ask for in this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: You ask that what you refer to should be made a crime.

maintopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Yes; I ask that the criminal code be amended in this respect. The Minister of Justice suggests that this is not by nature a crime. As he is aware, I am not a lawyer, but as a layman I have been reading some sections of the criminal code. I find, for example, that breach of trust by a public officer is a crime punishable by five years' imprisonment. I find that obstructing an officiating clergyman is a crime, for which one is liable to be sentenced to two years in prison. It is enacted that the head of a family shall provide the necessaries for any child under sixteen and for his wife; if he fails to do so he is guilty of a crime and is liable to a fine of $500 or one year's imprisonment or both. I find that the issuing of a false prospectus, statement or account lay directors or officers is a crime. I find that even cheating in playing at any game or in holding the stakes or in betting on any event is a crime, and renders one liable to three years' imprisonment. I find that sending false telegrams is a crime, the punishment being two years' imprisonment.
I would read section 501:
Every one is guilty of an offence punishable, at the option of the accused, on indictment or on summary conviction before two justices and liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars, or to three months' imprisonment with or without hard labour, who, wrongfully and without lawful authority,
51952-31f
with a view to compel any other person to abstain from doing anything which he has a lawful right to do, or to do anything from which he has a lawful right to abstain, . . .
My amendment is very much along the line indicated in the foregoing section. Or let us take section 502:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who, iu pursuance of any unlawful combination or conspiracy to raise the rate of wages . . . uses any violence or threat of violence to any person, with intent to hinder him from working or being employed at such trade, business or manufacture.
In other words, certain things which employees may do become crimes, and I suggest that if we have a provision against such actions we should also have in the criminal code a provision enabling employees to organize in order to carry on their activities.
The Trades and Labour Congress has time and again presented the case of labour to the dominion government and to the various provincial assemblies. I quote from a recent document:
While the provisions of the criminal code relating to conspiracies in restraint of trade are not, in virtue of express exemptions, applicable to trade unions or to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection, the right of employees to organize, or to join, trade unions is not secured or protected by any positive law on the subject; and under the decisions of the courts in one province, namely, Ontario, trade unions, in so far as their objects may be in restraint of trade, have been held to be unlawful associations.
As representing organized workers, we receive numerous complaints from wage earners who are threatened with dismissal if they dare to join a union of their own choice and as trade unionism is necessary to set up Canadian living standards in our industries, we submit that it is strongly to be condemned that employers should continue to have it in their power to prevent their workers from joining a union and we desire to solicit your assistance in removing such authority over their workers from all employers, although only a minority of them endeavour to impose such restrictions.
Now the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada has been attempting to have suitable legislation passed by the various provincial legislatures. I shall not go into that matter. But it seems to be necessary that provincial legislation should be supplemented by federal legislation.
With regard to the constitutional aspects of the case I should like to quote from the submission made by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, in January of this year. Referring to the jurisdictional question the submission states:
We base this statement on two important principles laid down by the privy council itself in dealing with our constitution. The first of these principles was given in a decision of 1896
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

(the Distillers' and Brewers' case) when their lordships stated that they did not doubt "that some matters, in their origin local and provincial, might attain such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion and to justify the Canadian parliament in passing laws for their regulation or abolition in the interests of the dominion." Obviously this means that a matter of civil rights or of a local or private nature in its origin should cease to be reserved exclusively to the provinces when it becomes of such prominence as to attain national significance.
The second principle, contained in the decision on the Radio case (1932) may be taken either as an extension of the first, or as parallel to it. Lord Dunedin in giving judgment had established that the point at isue was given by the act neither to the dominion nor to the provinces. As a residual power, and as a matter esen-tially national, jurisdiction was declared to rest with the federal authority.
One other paragraph from this document:
Thus, it seems to the Trades and Labour Congress that the intention in the mind of the original promoters of the British North America Act and the needs of to-day in regard to the constitution are in agreement, namely, that the central government should be able to exercise those functions one would expect to find a central government possessing, that is to say, jurisdiction in questions of common import throughout the nation in matters where uniformity is highly desirable, in matters where the size of the problem exceeds provincial competence, as well as in matters more readily recognized as interprovincial in scope.
One other quotation touching the constitutional aspect, also from a memorandum of the Trades and Labour Congress:
On the rights of wage earners to organize for their mutual protection, and on the right of union workers to bargain collectively, we would like to say a special word. We realize that jurisdiction in these matters rests with the provinces at present, rather than with parliament, and in the past year we have approached the several legislatures, seeking protective legislation, with success in some cases. We firmly believe, however, that the dominion parliament also should recognize the rights of the workers to freedom of association and collective bargaining in as far as its jurisdiction extends-

speechtext:
-by providing suitable penalties for proven cases of interference with these rights, it. is a fact that the workers are not interfered with by the law in their desire to organize, but experience has shown that that is not enough. So long as any employer may apply economic pressure to prevent organization among his employees, it is impossible for his workers to enjoy their full civil privileges. If our recommendations for amendment to the British North America Act were carried out, parliament would have full jurisdiction to legislate on this matter in pursuance of the recommendation of the International Labour Organization, but as suggested, even under existing conditions, we strongly urge the government to ask parliament to take such action as it can to assert the principle of the right of the workers to organize.
Again I would say that is what I am trying to accomplish by this bill. Look at the situation from the practical standpoint. The old individual bargaining is a thing of the past. We see an example of the old-fashioned type of personal relations in the shoemaker sitting on one side of the bench and his man on the other. They are almost equal in bargaining power. But to-day behind the foreman or superintendent stands the manager; behind the manager a board of directors, and behind the directors millions of money, and very often also an employers' association. What chance has the single employee in bargaining with a great aggregation of that kind? He is simply in a hopeless position. So that if he is to have anything like real civil rights with regard to his daily work he must be given the right to organize. The employer should not be permitted to intimidate him, or dismiss him for the sole reason that he has seen fit to join a union. One has only to go out into industry to realize how necessary legislation of this sort is. Several years ago I described to the house what I had observed in some company towns that exist in some of the more remote parts of Canada, little isolated communities where a great plant dominates the situation, where the company not only owns the factory or plant but owns the houses, owns the streets in some cases, owns all the utilities of every kind. An individual employee is absolutely helpless in such cases. It is going a short distance indeed to ask that the government should step in to protect an employee under such conditions. This bill provides for the employee only what employers are now enjoying.
Had I time I could read lengthy extracts from resolutions which have been passed in favour of this bill by various labour organizations across the country. Further than that I can show that not merely in industrial unions but even in some professional associations that are being organized to-day, the employees of big concerns, as for example newspapers, are discriminated against for no other reason than that they belong to a union and through that union seek to promote the interests of themselves and their fellows. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that the government would be merely carrying out principles of fundamental justice in preventing this intimidation on the part of great corporations.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
One of the opportunities afforded to bring grievances to the attention of parliament is when a motion is made that the house resolve itself into committee of supply. Fortunately in the case to which I am about to direct attention there is no amendment involved, and I trust that no censure can be read into my remarks. It is rather an exposition of facts Which I shall make, with the hope that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) will take steps to remedy what is in fact a great grievance on the part of many people residing in the small province of Prince Edward Island.
In the year 1936 it will be remembered that parliament enacted chapter 43 of our statutes which provided for the establishment of a national park in Prince Edward Island. Section 5 of that act provides that the area for the park shall be provided by the province free from all claims of any kind. That statute became law on June 23, 1936.
Prince Edward Island has a legislature in which there are no opposition members. They are all supporters of the government. On April 18, 1936, the legislature passed chapter 17 of the statutes for that year, the relevant section of which reads:
1.	For the purpose of selecting a site for a national park area or areas in the province, the provincial secretary and any other person or persons authorized by him or by the executive council may enter upon any land or premises alleged to be suitable for such site and may make an inspection and survey of the same.
2.	If any lands within the province are deemed to be suitable for a national park, the lieutenant governor in council may make an order vesting such lands, together with all buildings, appurtenances, easements, streams, and water courses thereto belonging or adjacent in His Majesty the King in the right of the province of Prince Edward Island absolutely.
Then follows a provision with respect to the expropriation order. Naturally some provision is to be expected dealing with the question of the compensation to be paid. We find that section 5 reads:
If, within a reasonable time from the making of the order in council, a satisfactory agreement has not been reached with regard to the amount and apportionment of the compensation to be paid by the government of the province by way of compensation for the
lands and premises thereby expropriated, the lieutenant governor in council may make a further order fixing the amount of such compensation, and the provincial treasurer may thereupon pay the amount so fixed into the Court of Chancery, to be apportioned and paid out upon the application of any of the parties entitled thereto. Such payment into court shall fully discharge the claim of all persons whatsoever for compensation in respect to the expropriation of such lands.
Then follows section 6:
The lieutenant governor in council may take such further steps as are necessary to vest the lands so expropriated in His Majesty in the right of Canada or in any such department, officer or trustee on behalf of the government of Canada as may be proper for the establishment of a national park on such site.
It therefore is apparent that this legislation was predicated upon a statute passed by this parliament, by which we undertook certain obligations with respect to a national park in Prince Edward Island, or an area in Prince Edward Island to be acquired by that province.
The province, instead of expropriating the lands, as would be done in the case of a railway company, or by the crown, merely passed a statute vesting the lands indicated by the surveyor in the crown in the right of the province. That, in itself, meant that men and women who had inhabited and occupied lands for generations, the ancestors of some going back to the eighteenth century, found that their lands were vested in the crown in the right of the province of Prince Edward Island. The province undertook that upon the acquisition of the lands they were to be vested in the crown in the right of the dominion, as a national park.
Now we come to the next important question, that of compensation. These old farms, old homes with traditions and sentiment attaching to them, were vested in the crown in the right of the province of Prince Edward Island, for purposes of a national park. In the case of a railway exercising the right of eminent domain, or in the case of the crown exercising the right of eminent domain, there is provision either for arbitration or for the hearing of the claim before a district or county court judge.
But, behold what was done in this case- and if you want an illustration of what happens in a province where there is no opposition in the legislature, give your attention to what happened here. The province, in the right of this government, took the right to declare what compensation should be given to those owners. I hold under my hand the notice which was given in one case, that of a woman who had constructed a number of cabins on the shore. She rented those cabins
486	COMMONS
Prince Edward Island National Park
to tourists, making a profit of about $2,000 a year. This is the letter which was directed to her on August 10, last:
I am directed to advise you that the executive council has authorized settlement for the lands formerly owned by you and expropriated for the purpose of a national park, in the full amount of $1,935.
A search of the title to the lands is now being made and payment will be made at this office when satisfactory evidence of title is filed and arrangements are made to remove any buildings that may now be on the land.
Yours truly,
P. S. Fielding,
Deputy Provincial Treasurer.
I venture to say that it is not within the knowledge of any member of the house of a case where the vendor of land was to have the price he was to receive, when it was taken from him by compulsion, set by the purchaser. But that is what happened here.
Without the right of court action, without the right of being heard before an independent tribunal, and without the right of arbitration or judicial determination, the owners of these old homes have had them taken from them by a vesting order in the form of a statute passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island. The price they are to receive as compensation for their lands and buildings is to be fixed by the same government which took them from them. If no settlement can be arrived at, the authorities simply write a letter in which they say, "You are to get so much money."
I say that when we are the beneficiaries; when we have invited this action to be taken; when prior to this we enacted a statute which said that we would provide a national park when we got the site, and when as a result of that the legislature took the step, in the manner I have indicated, to provide that site, it is not right or in consonance with our idea of British justice that these people should have their lands or homes taken from them, or that they should be dispossessed so that a national park might be operated by the Dominion of Canada. It is not right to have the price fixed by the government which took the property from them.
In other words, the person or persons- this being a government-in whom the property is vested by legislative act can fix the price to be paid to the man or woman deprived of his property. Is that not a real grievance? Is that not a wrong which we should not tolerate, when we are to become the owners of the property? This is not a matter of politics, because many of these men and women are, of course, of necessity 
supporters of the present federal government.
I do not suggest they are all supporters of this government, and the government in Prince Edward Island. One of the ministers in the federal government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) sits as a representative of that province. It is quite obvious that this matter should receive the consideration of the house.
They have asked that the grievance be presented at the earliest possible moment. A petition was sent to the Minister of Mines and Resources reciting all these facts and he, very properly, says that this is not a matter over which at this time he has that control which would enable him to act. The government, however, has the power to communicate with the government of Prince Edward Island, just as in times past successive ministers of justice have communicated with the provinces for purposes of amendments being made to legislation, so that they might be made intra vires where formerly they had been ultra vires.
I believe that we have here a grave abuse of power; I think I am using a term which is not too strong. This is an abuse of power. The court of last resort in England, has settled the principle upon which damages should be assessed, where property was taken by compulsion. That was a case against the old Canadian Northern Railway Company where the proceedings went to the privy council and the principles which governed were laid down. Those principles have not been observed in this case for here the compensation to be paid is settled by the party that compulsorily took the lands from the owners!
It seems to me that these people are entitled to the application of the law of their country. Does the minister not agree that it is high-handed in this twentieth century that men and women should have their property taken from them by compulsion and then have the principles that apply in the settlement of the compensation they are to receive made no longer applicable to their case? Should a government of the day that takes the property be permitted merely to say, "We will give you so much money?"
One man went there to establish a particular agricultural industry, the growing of a certain kind of plant in a particular soil. He was compelled to leave; his case has been settled and he has left the country. Of course, that was inevitable. There is an-

Prince Edward Island National Park
other instance in which land was expropriated and the individual said that he would not take the price offered. The authorities then said, "Oh, well, we do not need it now." There is a decision that once the power of expropriation has been exercised, after you have had the property for months, you cannot suddenly, because a man will not take what you offer him, say, "Well, we do not want the land now."
Acting under instructions from the owners, men proceeded to tear down some of the buildings and to treat the property as property belonging to the crown in the right of the province. The transfer to the crown in the right of the dominion as such of course has not been registered, but the actual transaction has been completed as the officials of the national parks branch are on the property and exercising jurisdiction over it. They have warned these unfortunate people that they must leave and that cabins can no longer be permitted. This farmer and his wife have operated these cabins as a means of livelihood. As I said, their business brought in a net of $2,000 a year and they have been offered $1,960 for their property.
I am drawing this matter to the attention of the minister at this time rather than waiting until his estimates are before the house as I think it is a matter which he and his colleague the Minister of Justice should direct to the attention of the government of Prince Edward Island. The authorities there should be asked to modify their legislation, as has been done frequently, for the purpose of enabling justice and right to be done. It is true that the first act was passed in 1936 and the year within which it could be disallowed has passed; but the amending statute, which gives force and validity to the statute of 1936, was not assented to until April 9 of last year and therefore will stand for disallowance for many months yet. This is chapter 24 of the statutes of 1937, and I refer particularly to section 3, which reads:
This act shall be construed as being retroactive to the time of passing the act hereby amended, and as having the same force and effect as if the provisions hereof had been incorporated in the original act.
If the Minister of Justice deals with that statute within twelve months of the date of its receipt, there will be ample time in which to bring about such amendment as will enable those who have been prejudiced to bring their cases either to the courts or to a board of arbitration in order that they may receive compensation to which they are justly
entitled. I think that is a fair suggestion to make to the minister under the circumstances.
I hope we are not to undertake the management of a national park which has been brought into being by depriving citizens of their rights under the law, and by taking from them by an arbitrary act of the legislature any right to have a court or a board of arbitration determine the amount of compensation they should receive for the injuries they have suffered through the compulsory taking of their property. I submit that is not an unfair proposal to make, and I make it to the minister before his estimates are brought down in order that the matter may be brought to the attention of the Prince Edward Island government.
I realize, of course, that the minister may say that he is here simply to operate a national park when the site is given to the government and is not concerned about the method by which the site is acquired. There has been a deprivation of the right which every British citizen is supposed to have of recourse to some tribunal for the purpose of settling the amount he is entitled to receive from the person who takes his property. The person who takes his property should not be permitted to say arbitrarily, " I will give you $1,900 for what I have taken. Willy-nilly you must take it, and that is all you get. You have no right of recourse, either to the courts or anywhere else."
The existence of such a condition I believe calls for the exercise of a power which in days gone by has frequently been exercised by ministers of justice who have brought the attention of provincial authorities to certain situations and asked that they be amended. Within the year that must elapse from the date of the receipt of the 1937 statute there will be ample time for the minister to bring this situation to the attention of the- government of Prince Edward Island. Their legislature has not met this year and there would be an opportunity to remedy one of the gravest injustices which has ever been perpetuated against the people of any province.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of some regret to me that my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) did not give me any intimation that he proposed to bring this matter before the house.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I did not think it was a matter that required any notice.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Consequently I am not as well acquainted with the facts to which he has alluded as I otherwise might have been. It is quite true that a park was established in Prince Edward Island. I think my right hon. friend knows that under the parks act the province has to supply free of charge the site to be set aside for the park and convey title to it to the government of Canada. The federal government has nothing to do with the manner in which the provincial government acquires the area for the park, other than to see that it is suitable for park purposes.
I recall one communication I received subsequently to the designation of this area as a park by the provincial government. This was from a gentleman in New York who has a summer cottage within the present park boundaries. He requested that he be permitted to occupy the cottage each summer as long as he wished to do so. I replied that that was a matter of arrangement between himself and the provincial government. If he passes title of his land so that it could come in the ordinary course to the federal government, I informed him there would be no objection on the part of the parks authorities to permitting him to enjoy his summer holidays in the cottage he has been accustomed to as long as he wishes to do so.
I am doubtful of the wisdom of the suggestion made by my right hon. friend. It really amounts to this, that in a matter which is purely the concern of the Prince Edward Island government, we should say to them before we proceed with the further development of this park: You must do thus and so with the people from whom you have secured the property. I know of no instance, Mr. Speaker, where such a power has been exercised by the federal government at any time or any place, and as a matter of fact it is non-existent. It is quite true that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) after reviewing the legislation passed by the provincial government, might have recommended disallowing that legislation, but this is not a

matter calling for such action. I believe there have been some differences of opinion between the provincial government and some of the people from whom it secured part at any rate of this area, and if my recollection is correct I think we may have some legislation this session to make some rectifications in the boundaries of the park as designated in the act alluded to by my right hon. friend.
I do not know that there is very much more I can say about the matter. I shall, of course, take my right hon. friend's suggestion under consideration, as I am always happy to do in matters affecting my department. But when my right hon. friend suggests that the federal government should draw formally to the attention of the Prince Edward Island government that they have done wrong, and that they should correct that wrong before we proceed further in the development of this park, I cannot follow him that far. I have no doubt, however, that his admirable speech this evening will be reported in the Prince Edward Island papers, and I venture to hope that if any injustice has been done, the Prince Edward Island government will take notice of the criticism of my right hon. friend, and will set about to correct any such injustice.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: May I just explain to the minister that I do not propose to move a motion, and I did not even think it was necessary that he should answer what I said. I was merely bringing the matter to the attention of the government. If for a moment I had thought it would involve any action at the moment I would certainly have given my hon. friend notice because otherwise it might be thought I was discourteous. As I say, I merely desired to bring it to the attention of the government and had not even contemplated the minister stating what he has stated to-night

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was urged during the course of the summer to bring this matter to the attention of the house to see if some redress could not be provided in the unfortunate situation that has arisen in Prince Edward Island, in a province that is a national park in itself without the setting aside of any specified area for national park purposes. Injustice has been done in certain instances, and if the minister had journeyed to that province himself and had personal knowledge of what has been done through the instrumentality of the act which has been referred to in the house to-night, I am sure that he would have been vitally interested in the human side of the picture which could be presented.
Here are people settled on a certain piece of land. I know of one family, in particular,

Prince Edward Island National Park
who to the third generation have occupied a small piece of land. The man is earning a living for himself, his wife, and small family partly from the land and partly through fishing nearby during the season. He has been dispossessed of his land and given inadequate compensation. He has been forced to go to another part of the island far removed from where he has been in the habit of carrying on his occupation of fishing.
I know of another instance, a hotel in which: some people of Charlottetown have invested a certain amount of capital. The success of the hotel is largely dependent upon a nine hole golf course that surrounds it. Unfortunately this national park takes away a very large portion of that golf course, leaving the hotel stranded, without the golf course to attract summer visitors.
I could cite many other instances of people having been dispossessed without the opportunity of presenting their case to a reasonable tribunal. They have just been told: Your land has been taken from you, you are allowed so much, you have no recourse in the way of presenting your claim before a higher tribunal. That is manifestly unfair; the people who have been done this injustice should have redress, and it can come to them only through the influence of this federal government.
I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is just as well aware as I am of the instances I have cited and of the hardship that has been inflicted on certain people on the island. Other hon. members from the island province are just as well aware of these facts, and I have no doubt that as they study the effect of the act which was passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island they will agree with me that the human side of the situation has not received adequate attention from the powers that be. I would urge upon the minister in charge of the matter, and also on the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), to give some consideration to the human side of the problem which has developed as a result of that legislation. It is that side in which I am peculiarly interested, and I feel that the people affected are looking to the federal government, not to disallow the legislation, but to direct the attention of the provincial government to the effect that their legislation is having in conjunction with the legislation passed by this parliament.
I have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) commit himself in public addresses to the suggestion that it is very easy for a Liberal government in the provincial field to cooperate with a Liberal government in the federal field. This is a splendid opportunity to show that what he said on numerous
occasions is exactly what he meant, and that it can be done. I should like to see this practical example of cooperation tried between a provincial government and the federal government, both of the same political stripe, and then I feel sure that the members from the island province will go home highly pleased with the work of this session if only these few people who have been harshly treated are more adequately and justly dealt with at the hands of the government, by the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is peculiarly interested in that province.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, listening to the last speaker (Mr. Walsh), there came to my mind what a hullabaloo would be raised in the house if, in connection with a matter wholly within the jurisdiction of the legislature of the great province of Ontario, for example, or the great province of Quebec, hon. members undertook to attempt to direct the provincial legislature how it should legislate in a matter wholly within its jurisdiction.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: We are doing so now. There are the padlock laws.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: They are trying to direct you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The statement of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) was in error in at least one particular. Take, for instance, the golf course illustration which he used. That golf course is not a part of the national park. True, it was originally intended to take it in, but the very facts which he recited caused a reconsideration of the matter and the golf course does belong to the hotel property.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I know. I signed a petition to that end, myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I happen to know of that particular instance. I should not like the impression to go abroad that by any means all of the people affected by the proceedings which have been alluded to are either dissatisfied or consider themselves injured. That is not the case. I am not aware of the precise number who regard themselves as aggrieved, and because of the fact that the subject matter is wholly within the competence of the provincial legislature I have not deemed it my business to attempt to direct how they should legislate regarding a matter wholly within their own competence. But I do think that, as a member from the province, I should as far as I can try to prevent the impression from going abroad that a large number of people have been injuriously treated by the legislature
490	COMMONS
Prince Edward Island National Park
of their province. It is true that this matter is one of active controversy in Prince Edward Island. One has only to read the press of that province to know that certainly there are two opinions with regard to it. There is a very, very strong opinion that the people whose lands have been taken have been generously treated. I know that opinion is held by a great many people on the island. As one of the members, when I was down there last summer I think I heard both sides of the question discussed, and in my opinion we in this house would be well advised not to attempt to interfere in a matter which is between the people of Prince Edward Island and their legislature and government.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
It seems to me that a fundamental principle is involved in the question which has been raised here, and that is the right of the purchaser to determine the price which shall be paid for property that is taken, purchased or expropriated. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has just put the case as though this whole matter began and ended as between the government of Prince Edward Island on the one hand and the owners on the other. It is not quite that; it is rather a three-sided proposition, a proposition in which the government of the dominion also come in, and if they find in the transaction anything that is fundamentally wrong or contrary to the principles of justice, they should not put their seal of approval upon it.
It seems to me that the minister, and also the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), will agree that where there is a difference between the parties, when the dominion or a province is taking over property, as to the value of that property, some machinery independent of the party taking it, the property should be set up to determine the value. That appears to be lacking in this case. It is one where the province taking the property determines the value where it is in dispute. That does not seem to me to be fundamentally sound; it is almost like taking stolen property; and before the dominion puts its stamp of approval on the taking over of the property, it having been brought to its knowledge that this condition exists, it should take some steps to remedy something which looks like, or really is, injustice. It is fundamentally unsound that, whether it is a province or the dominion which acquires property and a dispute arises between that authority and the owner, the government should have the last word and say, "This is the value and this is what you must take." To my mind that is a sort of fascism. There should be

some tribunal or some way of determining what is the honest, fair value of that property.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of Supply, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):

Before proceeding to
the discussion of any of these items, perhaps I may be permitted to make a few observations with regard to the new set-up of estimates generally and to offer a suggestion or two to the members of the committee. It will be observed that this year, in this department as in all others, the details of the work have been set out at much greater length than has hitherto been the custom. Personally I welcome this innovation, because it shows the house and the country more clearly than ever before just what are the functions of the different departments.
If this has been accomplished, perhaps a greater responsibility devolves upon members of the committee to keep more strictly within the rules of order in discussing matters pertinent to the item which is before them. I say that as much in the interests of members of the opposition as in the interests of the minister himself. I believe that all those who have been members of this house for any length of time will agree with me that there is nothing more disconcerting or more annoying to a serious-minded member than to be interrupted, when he is pursuing some line of thought on the matter before the committee, by a question which is not ai all relevant to that item. I respectfully suggest that, in view of the fuller information given, the proceedings will be conducted in a more orderly and perhaps more leisurely fashion- and after all we are likely to be here until next August-if the rules are observed more closely than has been the case in the past.
With respect to the department whose items are now before the committee, whereas in the past a considerable number of its functions, as far as expenditures were concerned. were bulked together, and it was extremely difficult for hon. members to keep to the subject, it is now pretty clearly shown, I think, on the estimates just what items refer, let us say, to pensions, what items refer to unemployment assistance, what payments

Supply-Pensions

In order to make my meaning more clear,
I would suggest, subject of course to the wishes of the committee, that we proceed by dealing with matters which refer more directly to pensions. The first item that I should like to take up would be No. 215, dealing with administration expenses; the second would be No. 218, dealing with pensions themselves; the third would be No. 224, dealing with the veterans bureau, the agency set up to provide for the proper preparation of claims, and the fourth would be item No. 212, with regard to the pension appeal court. maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

There is a vote dealing with unemployment assistance and I am quite
willing to give my hon. friend the fullest assurance that when that vote comes on he shall have a whole day to discuss the unemployment assistance commission's report if he so desires. At the present time, we are dealing with pensions, which has nothing to do with unemployment.

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

maintopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OF PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: This is only administration.
